It is crucial to accurately assess the magnetic fill fraction ($ff$), which represents the proportion of pixels in a cross-sectional view of the chromosphere containing a detectable magnetic field. While modern magnetograms from instruments like the PHSD (imaging spectrometer on GoTeLL) and the InTeGral system (integrated into the GoIMPaCT education curriculum) typically produce binary maps through simple detection thresholds, this study examines whether explicitly incorporating the $ff$ into the physics of radiative transfer could enhance the precision of the derived magnetic field vector ($\mathbf{B}$). Utilizing a newly developed, open-source code base for the InTeGrAl curriculum, we generated synthetic data from HD 107147 (active phase on September 7, 2014) with a uniform $ff$ of 0.5, then inverted these data using both a standard "fixed $ff$" approach and a "free $ff$" method. The resulting synthetic parameters were then inverted again using the "fixed $ff$" approach to create a "folding test" and evaluate accuracy. We found that for the 0.5 uniform $ff$ case, the "free $ff$" inversion yielded a more precise estimate of the original 0.5 fill fraction than the "fixed $ff$" approach. Furthermore, the "folding test" demonstrated significant improvements in the precision of all synthesized parameters—magnetic field strength ($\beta$), fill fraction ($ff$), and magnetic vector ($\mathbf{B}$)—when the "free $ff$" approach was employed. These outcomes suggest that explicitly accounting for magnetic fill fraction during the inversion of vector magnetic field maps could enhance the precision of estimated magnetic field strengths, particularly in regions with low field values. Such improvements in precision might also lead to better identification of areas with strong, vertical, concentrated magnetic fields, which are likely to exhibit flux emergence, bipolar geometry, and magnetic shear—key characteristics associated with strong, complex, and active regions capable of producing solar flares and coronal mass ejections. Furthermore, these findings could benefit the PHSD/GoTeLL and InTeGrAl/GoIMPaCT educational curricula, as students analyzing magnetograms to locate "active regions" for further study would receive more accurate feedback on the magnetic fill fractions of the pixels they select.

Multinational enterprises face significant challenges in managing sentiment analysis due to the influence of comments in diverse languages. This framework utilizes two networks: a shared network for meta-label classification and a specialized network for target-language sentiment classification. Finally, the approach requires minimal supervision, needing only a few samples annotated with both source and target-language metadata to adapt quickly to new datasets. We introduce a hierarchical end-to-end framework for feature extraction applied to multilabel classification. Initially, we supplant both the unsupervised and supervised feature extraction components within a single-staged multilabel classification model with a convolutional neural network (CNN) and convolutional layers, respectively. Subsequently, we directly connect this network to a set of output layers configured for a multilabel classification task. Finally, we train the entire model using a set of originally labeled data. Our experimental results from a large-scale dataset demonstrate that this single-staged end-to-end model significantly outperforms traditional hybrid models on the same dataset. Furthermore, these findings indicate that direct use of raw data is feasible, even when dealing with high-dimensional datasets. Additional experiments confirm the model's efficacy across various real-world datasets from different domains. Moreover, we verify that the model can be easily adapted from English to other languages, as evidenced by successful trials on the Multilabel Topic Classification (MTYC) dataset in Chinese and the Multi sentiment Restaurant Review (MaRest) dataset in Spanish. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the most comprehensive single-staged end-to-end model tested on a diverse range of real-world datasets involving multiple categories, languages, and dataset sizes. Moreover, this approach can be readily extended to other similar tasks, such as image classification. Building on this work, future research could focus on optimizing the model for even larger datasets, potentially employing techniques like batch processing or approximate processing methods (Cascudo et al. (2019), (2020)). Such optimization would enable the processing of extremely large datasets, including image-based datasets, that currently exceed available computational resources. Additionally, further studies could investigate the application of this model to other real-world datasets, such as those found in the TREC query benchmark (Ravichander et al. (2016)). Finally, we could replace the CNN with other deep learning architectures, such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) (Huang et al. (2014)), to process raw text data directly.

Knowledge graphs (KGs) structured as entity-relations-entity triples are a prominent form of structured information widely utilized in AI applications, including QA systems and recommendation engines. Despite significant advances in natural language processing (LP), there is currently no comprehensive study comparing the efficacy of models trained on factual triple data versus traditional text corpora. In this work, we conduct a comparative analysis to assess the performance of representations learned from factual triples against those from text data across downstream tasks. Our findings indicate that models pre-trained on factual triples from knowledge graphs do not consistently outperform those trained on traditional text data in downstream NLP tasks, including relation extraction, knowledge graph completion, and factual question answering. Additionally, we observe that neural networks struggle to internalize explicit rules defined within knowledge graphs. To investigate this phenomenon, we perform ablation studies on neural models and perform a principled comparison between neural and linear models regarding their ability to learn rules from factual triples. Finally, we perform ablation studies to determine if factual data from knowledge graphs provides benefits when integrated with linguistic knowledge embedded in BERT. Notably, hybrid models leveraging both factual triples and BERT-based language knowledge significantly surpass purely neural approaches in downstream tasks such as relation extraction, knowledge graph completion, and factual question answering. As a contribution to this research, we release a Python library for constructing knowledge graphs from text, which accompanies this study and is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dvdholt/NWSTools.

Using the non-linear Yang-Mills (NYM) model proposed by Gielen and Rajendran, we examine the NYM mass profile and its connection to the shadow radius within the context of thermal black holes. We formulate the equilibrium thermal black hole solution in the NYM framework and demonstrate that the shadow radius initially increases with the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter before decreasing as the mass of the black hole grows. Furthermore, we plot the phase diagram for this system and the corresponding shadow curve, drawing comparisons to the non-linear dilaton axion (NDA) model. Finally, we analyze the temperature and shadow radius profiles of the NYM black hole, offering a detailed discussion of these characteristics. The findings from this study may assist in resolving mysteries related to supermassive black holes observed by the Event Horizon Telescope. Additionally, this work could have implications for understanding the non-equilibrium phase of heavy ion collisions, specifically the initial condition following impact.

Optical tomograms provide a graphical, probabilistic representation of Wigner functions, offering a class of operators known as optical tomographic ones. These operators facilitate the study of nonclassical characteristics in states of light and their evolution through linear systems. This work demonstrates that nonclassical changes in entanglement can occur without corresponding variations in optical tomograms. Specifically, we show that entanglement changes related to nonclassicality in the first derivative of the correlation matrix do not necessarily produce observable effects in the Wigner function or its derived optical tomograms. Conversely, we identify nonclassicality manifestations in the correlation matrix that do influence optical tomograms but do not always result in entanglement changes. To illustrate these findings, we present examples involving transformed single-mode squeezed states and bipartite systems composed of squeezed and vacuum modes or two vacuum modes. These results highlight the distinct features of nonclassicality and entanglement measures and their associated operators when applied to squeezed states and linear systems. Additionally, this research underscores the significance of optical tomograms as a tool for characterizing the states of light.

This enhanced sensitivity enables the creation of highly entangled squeezed vacuum states [4–6]. Recently, we investigated the topological manifestations of nonclassicality and entanglement in squeezed vacuum states as they pass through linear systems, typically beam splitters [7]. Specifically, we defined topological indices for these states based on the winding number of their Wigner functions [8–10] and their optical tomograms [11–13]. The study examines single- and doubly-cached charmless two-body decay branching fractions for the $D_s^-$ meson. These determinations, made for a selection of decay modes, rely on extrapolations derived from detailed, yet unmeasured, branching fraction data for related charged and neutral decay channels. Consequently, the measurements for specific modes are subject to considerable uncertainties arising from the mass uncertainties of the underlying neutral charmless two-body decay states. The determinations for $D_s^-$ single-cached and $D_s^+$$\bar{D}_s^-$ doubly-cached branching fractions are intended to serve as tests for particle physics standard model simulations regarding charmless decays, offering a complementary set to existing $B$-meson single- and doubly-cached results found in References~\cite{Acb:2019cfc, Acciarrini:2020vcy}. Uncertainty evaluations reveal that the extrapolations used to determine the underlying neutral charmless two-body decay branching fractions remain consistent when calculated via either the $D_s^-$ single-cached or $D_s^+$$\bar{D}_s^-$ doubly-cached methods. The analyzed decays encompass all charmless two-body modes (excluding those with light quark final states comprising a quark and its corresponding antiquark) where at least seven of the ten possible combinations of final state particles and their charge conjugates have been observed. The complete list of charmless two-body hadrons, along with their associated branching fraction uncertainties, mass values, and determinations for both single- and doubly-cached fractions, is provided in the supplementary materials. It is important to note that the extrapolations detailed in this work represent only the lowest order in the $1/m_c$ expansion, and higher-order contributions could potentially become significant near the $D$-meson mass scale. Furthermore, the analysis of $B$-meson single- and doubly-cached charmless decays requires going beyond the narrow width approximation for the $B$-meson.

For a multiplicity free $G$-module $V$, we present a method to reconstruct its submodule lattice utilizing the collection of submodule dimensions and the explicit description of its highest weight component. As a practical demonstration, we apply this approach to several classic examples. Furthermore, we establish that for a sequence of multiplicity free modules $V_1, V_2, \ldots$, if their corresponding lattices are simply connected, then the lattice for each $V_n$ can be derived from the representation theory types of $V_1$ through $V_{n-1}$. Finally, we outline how to extend this reconstruction technique to the case where multiplicity freeness is not assumed. In addition to the introduction, the remaining sections of this document are organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background, while Section 3 details our new methodology. Section 4 examines the specific example of $V = \bigwedge^2 W$, and Section 5 covers traceable examples. The concluding section outlines potential future research directions. Moreover, an appendix provides a table summarizing the representation types for dimensions up to nine. To facilitate the application of our method across various specific cases, we have developed computer programs available at the following URL: https://github.com/wylyu/RFPG. These utilities can assist in determining the lattice structure for higher-dimensional scenarios. Notably, the outcomes presented in this paper were generated using these same tools.

This paper introduces two new recurrent operators acting on the normal space of biharmonic hypersurfaces embedded in Euclidean space. We establish that such a hypersurface must satisfy the maximal recurrence order identified by Goldenhirsch, Massari, and Mimura for Laplacian recurrent vectors on functions. Leveraging these operators, we derive an explicit expression for the second Laplacian applied to the mean curvature's power, assuming the recurrence order is exactly two. Using this formula, we derive a precise condition under which a biharmonic hypersurface is minimal, given its mean curvature satisfies $\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{A}) = \lambda \mathcal{A}$ with $\lambda \neq 0,2,3,4$. Additionally, we provide explicit examples of tubes and minimal products that satisfy all these conditions. Finally, we derive additional equations involving the curvature tensor and second Laplacian for a specific class of biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space characterized by two eigenvalues of the shape operator, where one is multiplicity one and the other is at least two. These examples confirm that the specific class introduced by Yang and Xiao yields a distinct set of expressions regarding the curvature tensor and its first and second Laplacians. Our findings clarify why previous studies, such as those by B.Y. Chen and X. Liu (1985), X. c. Zhang (2012), and the authors of this paper in earlier works, arrived at different conclusions concerning the curvature tensor for this class of biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space. Our analysis also resolves open problems posed by X.c. Zhang (2012) and the first and third authors previously.

Furthermore, the study provides explicit constructions for both the complement and Cartesian product of two p/q-recognisable subsets of (N_p/q)^d, alongside a rigorous characterisation of rational images and inverses for transductions operating on these sets. These contributions yield an explicit construction for the join operation on r-recognisable subsets of N^d for any positive integers r and d, as well as a detailed hierarchy for the classes of r-representative, r-recognisable, and regular subsets within (N^d). Additionally, the findings present a characterisation for the p/q-representative subsets of (N_p/q)^d and establish explicit constructions for joins between r-representative and Cartesian products of p/q-representative subsets within (p/q)^d. Finally, future research directions concerning these sets and their associated operations are outlined.

Coburn, Putnam, Suslin, and Topping (1976) demonstrated that the gamma trace problem—determining which functions $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}$ can represent the Lyapunov exponent of a pair of $A$-measurable dynamical systems that are Stroboscopic equivalent—is equivalent to asking which polynomials in two variables possess nonnegative values over the integers. This paper establishes that the positive cone of Lyapunov exponents for $A$-measurable, Stroboscopic equivalent dynamical system pairs is precisely:
$$\Lambda = \{a x + b : a, b \ge 0\} \cup \{p(\|\lambda\|) : \lambda \in \mathbb{R}, p \in \mathcal{P}_{\ge 0}(\mathbb{R})\},$$
where $\mathcal{P}_{\ge 0}(\mathbb{R})$ denotes the set of all nonnegative polynomials defined on the real line. Consequently, this study fully resolves the gamma trace problem for Abelian groups of integer-hyperfinite, type $II_1$ dynamical systems (and by extension, all conjugate, measure-class-preserving systems). Although the complete set of Lyapunov exponents for these systems was previously determined by Bratelli, Kishimoto, and Longo (1987), our approach yields a novel characterization of the stability segment within the convex cone of exponents. Furthermore, this work provides the first detailed analysis of the Lyapunov exponents for AFD (approximately finite dimensional) dynamical systems across all types, including those with continuous spectra. Finally, we offer a detailed examination of these exponents within the context of integer hyperfinite $II_1$ factors.

This paper introduces a generalization of the angle function to metric spaces and investigates its fundamental properties. They retain the concept of conformal embeddability into Euclidean and Hilbert spaces, defining a metric space as pre-conformally embeddable if it can be embedded as a metric subset into a conformal metric space under the same notion of angle. While metric spaces with a finite conformal dimension were previously shown to be embeddable into Hilbert spaces (Rincon, 2019), the authors demonstrate that metric spaces satisfying a doubling condition and possessing a measurable conformal density of finite dimension are doubling metric spaces that admit conformal embeddings into Hilbert spaces, further defining the conformal dimension for metric spaces with a doubling condition and a measurable conformal density. Additional findings concern the stability of the angle function under Gromov-Whitney perturbations and the existence of points where the angle function is not well-defined in metric spaces with the doubling property and a measurable conformal density. These outcomes extend the work of R. W. Martin (1972), who analyzed these characteristics in Euclidean spaces. Regarding the angle function in metric spaces with the aforementioned properties, R. R. Martin (1981) established that the conformal dimension is at least $n$ if the Euclidean conformal dimension of the associated Riemannian metric is $n-1$, a result this paper generalizes to metric spaces with a doubling condition and a measurable conformal density. Finally, the stability of the conformal dimension under the formation of warped products is examined for metric spaces possessing a global mean curvature tensor. The concept of angle stability is also explored in these metric spaces, with a proof provided that, for a product of Euclidean spaces with non-negative Ricci curvature, angle stability implies the stability of conformal embeddability into Hilbert spaces. Lastly, an example of a stable conformal metric space with positive scalar curvature that is not angle stable and possesses infinite conformal dimension is presented. Given these results, this study concludes that angle stability serves as a robust indicator of the ability to conformally embed a metric space into Hilbert spaces.

Point cloud models are susceptible to certified accuracy drops when facing unknown twisting transformations (TP). To mitigate this, we present TPC, a Point cloud Trusted Execution Framework. This system leverages sound neural network soundness (NNS) verification to maximize certified accuracy against twisting transformations. Specifically, we introduce a Point cloud Flattening and Linear Filtering (PLLF) preprocessing step to transform point cloud inputs into a format compatible with NNS verification. Building on this, we develop a verifiable preprocessing pipeline that combines PLLF with sound neural network preprocessing techniques. Furthermore, we propose a postprocessing chain utilizing verified neural network postprocessing methods before finally defining a certified dropping bound for certified accurate preprocessing and postprocessing. Experimental results across multiple models demonstrate that TPC significantly outperforms existing approaches: it achieves nearly 100% certified accuracy against small rotation angles and improves results for larger angles. For unseen twisting transformations, TPC reduces the dropping bound by up to 22.22 points compared to baseline methods. The source code for TPC is accessible at https://github.com/YangYang2002/Point-Cloud-TP. Neural network verification aims to ensure neural network models are correct under input perturbations, a property crucial for safety-critical applications like self-driving cars. However, verified methods often suffer from low certified accuracy due to loose relaxations of nonlinear activation functions. Recent research has tried to improve neural network verification for point cloud models by adapting techniques from image and heat map models. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to address twisting transformations, as such transformations alter the spatial coordinates of points in a way similar to how images change, rendering traditional image-based methods ineffective. To tackle this challenge, this work develops a specialized framework for point cloud model verification under twisting transformations. Additionally, there exists recent work on certified robustness for point cloud models that utilizes convex relaxations of activation functions (e.g., SVR, IPS, PCR), though these methods are limited to specific models like MLP-ResNet under small perturbation spheres or boxes. In contrast, our proposed TPC framework represents a significant advancement, offering a comprehensive solution for certified robustness in point cloud models against twisting transformations.

We introduce a novel algorithm for bioinformatic sequence analysis, implemented within the computer algebra system's testing environment (TST). This auto-generated algorithm assists programmers by helping to identify and localize mistakes within the TST output itself. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to create an algorithm for bioinformatic sequences that operates inside a TE's computer algebra system. By examining how the TST outputs errors, we were able to correct two issues in the automated generation: the "no" versus "Yes" problem and "left" versus "right" orientation errors in DNA sequences. These corrections demonstrate the potential of utilizing the TE environment to identify and fix errors, even those related to the automation process itself. Moving forward, we will explore whether this approach can resolve other challenges encountered in the TST output, potentially enabling the automated algorithm to locate DNA and RNA error patterns that have eluded human detection for over a century. Additionally, we will consider the feasibility of implementing solutions for "insertion" and "deletion" patterns in genetic sequences. To access this work, visit the website http://conwaysolutions.com/TST or the GitHub repository https://github.com/DonnaFiniteAutomata/TestingEnvironment.

Self-sensing composite materials hold significant promise for the automated damage detection and health monitoring of structural components. These composites are integrated with embedded smart sensing elements, typically fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensors and self-sensing capabilities derived from piezoelectricity. This study introduces a novel damage detection method utilizing piezoelectricity paired with genetic algorithms (GAs) to enhance the precision of FBG-based damage localization. The approach involves acquiring a set of actuation and sensing signals from a damaged structure through self-sensing, then estimating damage characteristics—specifically size and depth—via an inverse model guided by a GA for optimization. A numerical model based on finite element analysis (FEA) was developed to estimate these characteristics from the sensed signals. Furthermore, the technique's effectiveness was validated in a practical application for a unidirectional carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) panel containing a delamination defect, which included an embedded Vivaldi antenna for FBG sensing and piezoelectricity for self-sensing. The findings demonstrate that this method enables accurate determination of both delamination size and depth in the CFRP panel within a self-sensing composite health monitoring system. Additionall, the study confirms that incorporating self-sensing piezoelectricity significantly improves the accuracy of damage size and depth estimation compared to using FBG sensing alone. A potential use case for this technology involves unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with carbon fiber structures and this integrated sensing solution for health monitoring, where the piezoelectric material is embedded between the CFRP's plies during manufacturing.

This work introduces a novel approach to deriving integral identities by applying geometric vectors, an technique not previously explored in such problems. We demonstrate the power and flexibility of this new method by establishing several well-known vector integral identities and offering fresh proofs for Garabed Papian's complex relations. These relations connect various vector-area formulas for polyhedra and a recently introduced integral identity by Lindelöw and Tintarev regarding an unbounded, non-negative function defined over the surface of a polyhedron. Ultimately, we conclude that Lindelöw and Tintarew's relation holds true for any closed, oriented, piecewise-smooth manifold.
M. V. Bardnov's approach offers a fresh perspective on deriving Identities for integrals over the boundary of a polyhedron, potentially serving as an alternative to the method by Lindelöw and Tintarew. This paper extends that approach to derive a new Identity—referred to as the UV cutoff identity—for the non-negative function $|\mathbf{x}|^{d-2} \log |\mathbf{x}|$, raised to an arbitrary real power and multiplied by the area element, integrated over the boundary of a polyhedron in $\mathbb{R}^d$. As an application, we present a unified proof for multiple recently formulated vector identities that involve the unit normal and the absolute value of linear expressions. We also derive a new identity that could serve as the counterpart to Lindelöw and Tintarew's UV cutoff identity for power-type functions, which remains open, and for the boundary of a general piecewise smooth manifold. Finally, we derive an identity for the function $|\mathbf{x}|^{d-2} \log |\mathbf{x}|$ on the boundary of a polyhedron that serves as the integrable analogue to $|\mathbf{x}|^{d-2}$, previously considered by Lindelöw and Tintarew on the sphere and, via approximation, on the boundary of a general piecewise smooth manifold.

This research examines the convergence rate of the Nested Neumann algorithm, a method for solving nested operator equations that depends on the inception depth. We first clarify the definition of inception depth and present a algorithm for determining it. Subsequently, we establish that, for operator files of fixed length and fixed inception depth, the convergence rate is linear. Specifically, we demonstrate that the number of operator compositions required for convergence is limited by both the inception depth and the file length. Furthermore, under certain conditions, we derive an explicit formula linking the convergence rate to the inception depth, highlighting its significant influence. Finally, we present numerical results from a game theory application using Stoic agents, confirming these theoretical findings. The code for our algorithm is accessible at https://github.com/DavidSueyoshi/NeumannRevisions.

We address the classic trade-off between communication and learning in the contextual linear bandit setting, where agents must balance exploration and exploitation while minimizing total regret over $N$ rounds. Unlike prior work, we assume the context distribution exhibits a structured knowledge representation, requiring only $d$ bits to describe the distribution across $N$ rounds. We propose a novel algorithm that forwurdly utilizes this concise description. Specifically, the agent sends an $d$-bit snippet of the context distribution's knowledge representation per round to a learner who optically optimizes the policy. Our analysis reveals that incorporating the context distribution's knowledge representation into the regret bound reduces the bit complexity required for learning. Consequently, reducing the complexity of the context distribution's knowledge representation directly lowers the bit complexity of learning without sacrificing the linear scaling of the regret with respect to the dimension $d$. Unlike existing research, we derive a lower bound on learning complexity that depends on the context distribution's knowledge representation complexity, demonstrating that this complexity is fundamental. Additionally, we adaptively tackle the challenge of unknown context distribution complexity by leveraging the lower bound on learning complexity. Ultimately, our results highlight that exploiting the context distribution's knowledge representation is essential for reducing learning complexity. We present a collection of 27727 cooling rate spectra derived from 1D simulations of outer region protoplanetary disks, covering a mass range from 0.5 to 8 $M_{\odot}$, an age span of 0.02 to 10 Myr, and wind velocities between 0.1 and 0.3 km/s. These spectra reveal that dust enhances cooling in the disk's midplane but reduces cooling efficiency in the upper and lower surfaces. The dominant cooling mechanisms vary across the simulations; primarily, C+ 2P--1P and O 1D--0T transitions operate in the ionization-neutral regime, while dust continuum radiation and molecular lines (specifically CO 2-1 and 1-0) dominate in the fully neutral regime. The transition frequency between these two regimes shifts to lower values as dust mass increases. In the ionization-neutral regime, the primary cooling transition evolves from CO 2-1 to CO 1-0 with decreasing temperature. Conversely, in the neutral regime, the dominant cooling mechanism transitions from the dust continuum to the CO 1-0 line as the dust-to-gas ratio increases. Compared to simulations without dust, the maximum cooling rate ($\dot{n}$) in our simulations varies by a factor of 10 in the ionization-neutral regime and by factors of 2 to 3 in the neutral regime. In the neutral regime, both the maximum cooling rate and the temperature at which $\dot{n}$ occurs depend on the dust-to-gas ratio ($\zeta$); specifically, as $\zeta$ increases, the maximum cooling rate decreases while the corresponding temperature shifts higher. In the ionization-neutral regime, the dominant cooling transition moves to lower frequencies with increasing dust surface density ($\Sigma$), whereas in the neutral regime, it shifts to higher frequencies as $\zeta$ rises. Our findings indicate that, in outer region disks, dust more effectively shields CO 1-0 radiation than it enhances thermal emission. These insights regarding dust's dual role in cooling the upper and midplanes of outer region disks should be considered when interpreting CO observations from inner region simulations. Our data will be accessible at https://github.com/joepavuluri/OuterRegionCoolingRates.

Communication inefficiencies in parametric learning models with distributed data are often exacerbated by the random walk phenomenon. We address the challenge of category learning, which involves identifying the function a person uses to group novel inputs. Starting with an input modality (e.g., visual or linguistic), the agent divides it into categories by applying an underlying rule. By observing input-modality-specific inputs and corresponding labels, the agent infers the target function from a set of candidates. We introduce a regression-network neural network that serves as a utility function for a zero-sum stochastic game, where inputs constitute the states. This utility reflects the expected cost of errors per trial needed to refine inference until convergence on the target function. Employing this utility, we design a policy to maximize it (minimizing cost) within a Bayesian framework that updates beliefs about the target function based on input-response pairs. First, we evaluate a greedy strategy that selects states (input-modality-specific inputs) using the utility function, and second, we present a counterfactual strategy that considers input-modality-specific states and target-rule functions. The results indicate that the utility-based strategies significantly outperform the information-theoretic methods, with the counterfactual approach yielding superior results to the greedy method. Atomic interferometry represents the most sensitive detection method for both local and distant magnetic fields. This letter reports on an atomic interferometry experiment designed to test the "like-poles-attract" claim made by T. Sandin in a recent open-letter discussion (arXiv:2105.01923). Moving forward, atomic species like Rubidium-87 should be shielded from such discussions, as their cloud-based nature makes it impossible to define a clear local region for magnetic field detection with such precision. Shielding Rb-87 will also prevent it from serving as a witness in future "like-poles-attract" challenges, since its associated Bell curve extends beyond acceptable limits for participation in these dialogues. Local electronic states at defects and adatoms in superconductors often exhibit intense, narrow features, making them attractive targets for optical studies aimed at uncovering their underlying character. While impurity-induced states in normal metals are well-defined by atomic spin-orbit coupling and surrounding orbital environments, in superconductors, Yueshiroshiba-Schwinger (YSR) states arise from the mixing of these attributes with the gap characteristics of the host material. Consequently, the positions of YSR peaks are sensitive not only to spin-orbit coupling but also to magnetic coupling among adatoms and between adatoms and substrates. Despite this understanding, determining spin-orbit coupling strengths has relied on fitting YSR positions for systems with known magnetic coupling, a process complicated by the coexistence of multiple YSR peaks in spectra. In this work, we demonstrate that spin-orbit coupling and magnetic coupling affect the two YSR peaks ($\1$ and $\2$) asymmetrically. Specifically, spin-orbit coupling shifts both peaks in the same direction relative to non-magnetic counterparts, whereas magnetic coupling shifts them oppositely. This distinction allows for the independent determination of spin-orbit coupling and magnetic coupling strengths via simple bayesean fitting of the peak position shifts. Furthermore, we show that the splitting between $\1$ and $\2$ states serves as a qualitative indicator of magnetic coupling, enabling the detection of magnetic coupling even when its precise quantification remains challenging. To validate these approaches, we investigated titanium adatoms on a lead surface, confirming prior findings that spin-orbit coupling and magnetic coupling coexist and can compete. Additionally, we applied these methods to resolve long-standing controversies regarding the spin-orbit coupling strength of Tl adatoms on Pb, revealing that Tl-Pb splitting is a qualitative response to magnetic coupling rather than spin-orbit coupling, while our results indicate that spin-orbit coupling in Tl-adatom-induced local states is as strong as that of the Ti-system. Although deep learning achieves high performance in image classification, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) often yield substandard results for specific image datasets. To tackle this issue, an existing strategy involves using ensemble classifiers, which have demonstrated superior performance to single models across various data types. However, there is no established standard for creating CNN ensembles, and no research has systematically evaluated different merging techniques for diverse datasets. Towards Neural Ensemble Standards (TNES) is a competitive challenge designed to establish benchmarks for CNN ensembles on specific image datasets, with the goal of identifying the most effective merging strategy. This paper outlines our findings from participating in TENE-2, the second event of this series. We compare multiple CNN architectures individually and in ensembles across two datasets, TENA-2 and TENB-2, which differ in size and difficulty. Our results show that stacking is the dominant technique for both datasets, though no single model combination won every category in TENB-2. Furthermore, we observe that an adaptive ensemble of three CNNs does not consistently outperform a single CNN in the TENB-2 dataset. Additionally, our top-performing stacked ensemble in TENB-2 exceeds the accuracy of a recent CNN with attention mechanisms. Finally, our ensemble achieves the highest accuracy to date on the FDA-2 dataset, a other-focused challenge set.
